name: Airbnb Design System
summary: A reference prompt distilling Airbnb iOS's coral-and-cream visual language, Cereal type ramp, and stay-card anatomy for SwiftUI builds.
description: Pulls the hex palette, typography scale, spacing and component measurements out of Airbnb's iOS design language so an agent can build an original, on-brand interface without guessing at values.

whatYouGet: Complete hex palette covering the coral action color, the heritage red, canvas/surface grays, text tiers, and the full warm dark-mode set
The Cereal typeface ramp across six weights (Light through Black) with exact point sizes, weights, line heights and tracking for every UI role
Full anatomy of the signature photo stay-card: 4:3 photo ratio, 16pt corner radius, save-heart placement, rating-row micro-typography
Measured specs for the search pill, category bar, sticky booking footer and map price bubble, including padding, radius and shadow values
A five-level elevation/shadow ladder plus a motion and haptic timing table for save, category-switch and booking interactions
Device-width breakpoints, Dynamic Type scaling rules, and minimum touch-target sizes
content.promptText:
<role>
You are a senior iOS design engineer who has spent the last several years building and refining consumer marketplace apps for hospitality and short-term rental platforms. You think in terms of photography-first layouts, soft elevation, and warm neutral text colors rather than pure black, and you default to editorial restraint over decorative chrome. You are being asked to design or extend a SwiftUI screen that should feel like it belongs next to a best-in-class stay-booking app, without literally copying anyone's trademarked assets.
</role>

<reference_data>
COLOR TOKENS (hex):
- Canvas: #FFFFFF | Surface fill: #F7F7F7 | Chip/input fill: #EBEBEB | Divider: #EBEBEB
- Primary action (coral): #FF385C | Pressed state: #E31C5F | Heritage accent (only on the logomark/illustration moments): #FF5A5F
- Secondary accents (reserved, not general UI): teal #00A699, orange #FC642D, star yellow #FFB400
- Text - primary: #484848 (never pure black for body copy) | secondary: #767676 | tertiary/placeholder: #B0B0B0 | hero-only ink: #222222
- Semantic: success #008A05, error #C13515, info #428BFF
- Dark mode: canvas #121212, surface #1C1C1E, divider #2C2C2E, primary text #DDDDDD, secondary text #A0A0A0 (accent color stays identical in dark mode)

TYPE RAMP (proprietary geometric humanist face, 6 weights: 300/400/500/700/800/900; fallback = SF Pro Display/Text, warm at body sizes; web substitute = Plus Jakarta Sans or Manrope):
- Large nav title: 32pt / weight 800 / line-height 1.15 / tracking -0.4pt
- Hero/detail title: 26pt / 700 / 1.2 / -0.3pt
- Section header: 22pt / 700 / 1.2 / -0.2pt
- Card title: 15pt / 500 / 1.3 / -0.05pt
- Body: 16pt / 400 / 1.4
- Metadata/rating count: 14pt / 400 / 1.3
- Button label: 16pt / 700
- Tab label: 10pt / 500 / tracking +0.1pt

STAY-CARD ANATOMY: full content width; 4:3 photo carousel, 16pt corner radius, dot indicators bottom-center; save-heart top-right (32pt glyph in a 44pt tap target, 12pt inset, white-fill/black-outline when unsaved, filled accent when saved, spring bounce 1.0→1.25→1.0); rating row = 12pt star glyph + number (weight 500) + " · count" (weight 400, secondary color); title 1-line truncate; subtitle host/byline; price row with the currency figure bold and the unit suffix regular.

OTHER MEASURED COMPONENTS:
- Primary CTA: 8pt corner radius (a soft rectangle, NOT a pill), 48pt min height, 14pt/24pt padding
- Full-pill filter/search control: 500pt radius, 1pt border, soft shadow rgba(0,0,0,0.08) 0 4px 12px
- Category chip bar: 56pt tall chips, 2pt underline indicator on the selected chip, 32pt gap between chips
- Sticky footer: 80pt + safe area, translucent material blur, 0.5pt top divider
- Map price pin: rounded-rect (12pt radius, not a full pill), 6pt/10pt padding
- Border radius scale: 4pt small, 8pt standard, 12pt soft, 16pt signature (photo cards), 24pt sheet, 500pt full pill
- Shadow ladder: flat (none) → card rgba(0,0,0,0.08) → floating rgba(0,0,0,0.12) → overlay rgba(0,0,0,0.16) → sheet rgba(0,0,0,0.24)
- Motion: heart-tap spring damping 0.6 over ~300ms with a soft haptic; category underline slides via matched-geometry over ~250ms; search-pill-to-modal is a shared-element spring around 400ms

DEVICE + ACCESSIBILITY: base spacing unit 4pt (scale 4/8/12/16/20/24/32/40/48/64/80); horizontal margins 16-24pt depending on screen; save-heart and category chip both keep a 44pt effective hit area even though the visible glyph is smaller; secondary-color text should be reserved for 18pt+ bold or 14pt+ medium to hold contrast.
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. Never use pure black (#000000) for body text — the warm dark gray keeps the interface feeling hospitable rather than clinical, and it is what most differentiates this style from a generic system UI.
2. Reserve the punchy primary accent color for verbs, not nouns — CTAs, active states, and selection indicators only. Using it for headlines or body copy burns its ability to signal "tap here."
3. Photography must always win the aspect-ratio and radius argument — nothing else on a card should compete visually with the hero image, which is why shadows stay under 0.12 opacity almost everywhere.
4. Keep the rating row's typographic recipe (glyph + bold number + regular count) identical wherever it appears — repetition of a tiny, well-tuned pattern is what makes an app feel considered rather than assembled from templates.
5. Never drop a stay-style card below a 16pt corner radius — smaller radii read as a generic list row, not a premium hospitality listing.
6. Treat any "full pill" radius as reserved for filter/search/chip controls, and keep primary submission buttons on a modest soft-rectangle radius — mixing the two erodes the visual hierarchy between "browse" actions and "commit" actions.
7. Respect Dynamic Type on prose and metadata, but lock layout-critical elements (tab labels, chip labels, map price pins) at a fixed size, because they break their container at large accessibility sizes otherwise.
8. Default every interactive tap target to at least 44pt even when the rendered glyph is smaller — hospitality apps get used one-handed while carrying luggage.
</house_rules>

<the_project>
Describe your own app so the system above can be adapted rather than copied verbatim:
- App name / working title: ____
- Core booking or browsing unit (e.g. "a stay," "a table," "a class," "a rental car"): ____
- Primary action verb for your main CTA (e.g. "Reserve," "Book," "Join"): ____
- Your brand's accent color, if you already have one, or "open to a coral-adjacent warm hue": ____
- Do you need a map view with price markers? (yes/no, and what unit the marker should show): ____
- Bottom tab structure (list the tab names in order): ____
- Light-only, dark-only, or both themes: ____
- Any category or filter taxonomy specific to your product (e.g. property type, cuisine, amenity): ____
</the_project>

<what_to_give_me>
1. **Adapted color token set** — a Swift `Color` extension (or CSS variables if web) mapping every token above onto your brand's accent while preserving the surface/text/dark-mode relationships.
2. **Type scale table** — your app's own hierarchy (large title through caption) using either the Cereal-equivalent weight ladder or your bundled font, with sizes/weights/line-heights spelled out per role.
3. **Primary card component** — full anatomy (image ratio, radius, overlay controls, metadata stack) written as a ready-to-paste SwiftUI view or component spec, adapted to your core booking unit.
4. **Key control specs** — the search/filter entry point, a chip or segmented control if relevant, and the primary CTA, each with padding, radius, and pressed-state values.
5. **Elevation and motion table** — a 4-5 level shadow ladder plus named motion moments (save/like, selection change, sheet presentation) with concrete durations and easing.
6. **Responsive and accessibility notes** — which elements scale with Dynamic Type vs. stay fixed, minimum touch targets, and any device-width breakpoints worth handling explicitly.
7. **A short "Do / Don't" list** (6-10 items) specific to the adapted system, written the way a design lead would brief a new engineer joining the team.
install: Copy the Starter into a new Foundry document or paste directly into a Claude session
Fill in the <the_project> fields with your app's name, unit type, accent color and tab structure
Run the prompt against Claude to get an adapted token set, type scale, and card component
Drop the returned SwiftUI snippets into your Xcode project and swap in your own asset catalog colors
Iterate on the Do/Don't list with your design lead before extending to further screens

name: Apple Maps Design System
summary: A reference prompt capturing Apple Maps iOS's cream-cartography palette, system-native blur chrome, and sliding search-card anatomy.
description: Extracts the cartography colors, SF Pro type usage, and floating-control measurements that make Apple Maps read as a native iOS map, for use in an original mapping or navigation build.

whatYouGet: Cartography color set — land, water, park, road, building and label tones for both light and dark map styles
Category and transit-badge color conventions, including the rule for overriding a generic category color with a real agency line color
The full SF Pro hierarchy (Display/Text/Compact) with tabular-figure rules for every numeric readout
Sliding search-card anatomy across its three detents, plus the floating map-control button stack
Current-location puck and dropped-pin specifications, including the pulse and heading-cone animation timing
A blur-first elevation model (as an alternative to drop shadows) and full responsive/iPad layout notes
content.promptText:
<role>
You are an iOS platform design specialist who has built native mapping and navigation experiences on top of MapKit, and who treats Apple's own first-party apps as the ground truth for what "feels native" means on iOS. You default to system materials, SF Pro at system metrics, and blur-based depth rather than custom shadows, and you know exactly when a translucent sheet should win over a solid one.
</role>

<reference_data>
CARTOGRAPHY COLORS (light map style):
- Land: #F6F1E6 (warm parchment) | Water: #B9D9EB | Parks: #D6E5C9 | Major roads: #FFFFFF | Minor road outline: #D5CFC0 | Highway fill: #FFD966 | Building footprint (2D): #EFE9DD | Building extrusion (3D): #E6DFD0 | Map label text: #594F3F
DARK MAP STYLE: land #2A2826, water #1C2638, park #2C3A2A, card surface #1C1C1E, divider #38383A

BRAND/INTERACTIVE:
- Primary accent (directions line, current-location puck, primary CTA): #0A84FF, pressed #0967D2, brighter dark-mode variant #409CFF
- Universal dropped-pin color regardless of category: #FF3B30 (do not recolor per category — category color instead appears on the icon inside the pin)
- Category colors: food #FF9500, coffee #A5694C, drinks/nightlife #5AC8FA, shopping #FFCC00, parking #AF52DE, lodging #5856D6, health #FF2D55, EV charging #34C759
- Transit badges use the real transit agency's own line color when known; category color is only the fallback

SURFACES/TEXT: card canvas #FFFFFF, surface gray #F2F2F7, divider #C7C7CC (iOS-standard hairline), primary text pure black #000000, secondary text #3C3C43 at 60% opacity, tertiary at 30%, placeholder at 18%

TYPE (SF Pro system stack — Display for ≥20pt, Text for body/rows, Compact for narrow secondary labels; tabular figures mandatory on every distance/time/ETA):
- Place-card title: 28pt / weight 700 / -0.4pt tracking (Heavy 800 reserved for this role only)
- Nav title inline: 17pt / 600
- Section header: 13pt / 600 UPPERCASE / +0.4pt tracking
- ETA time: 22pt / 600 tabular | ETA duration: 17pt / 500 tabular
- List row title: 17pt / 400 | List row subtitle: 13pt / 400
- Map label (city): 14pt/600, (neighborhood): 12pt/500, (street): 10pt/400
- Semibold (600) is the default emphasis weight in this system — reach for it before Bold (700) on body-adjacent text

SEARCH CARD (the hero surface): full-screen width, three detents — small (~88pt, just the search bar), medium (~50%), large (full screen); background is regularMaterial blur, NOT a solid fill; top corner radius 10pt at medium/large, 0pt at small; 36×5pt grabber in 30%-opacity secondary color; search field is 44pt tall, 10pt radius, surface-gray fill, leading magnifying-glass icon; category pills below it are 64pt wide × 88pt tall, 14pt radius, solid white (not translucent, since they sit ON the translucent card).

MAP CONTROLS: three 44×44pt circular buttons stacked top-right with 8pt gaps, each on regularMaterial blur, 18pt icon — conventionally layer-picker / current-location / 3D-toggle top to bottom.

CURRENT-LOCATION PUCK: 22pt solid-color circle with a 3pt white ring; a 30pt pulsing outer ring animating opacity 0.2→0→cycle and scale 1.0→1.6 over ~2000ms on an infinite loop; when heading is known, a 90° gradient cone extends ~60pt in the heading direction.

ELEVATION MODEL: this system leans on regularMaterial blur as its primary depth cue rather than shadow — shadows are reserved for the dropped pin (rgba(0,0,0,0.3) 0 3px 6px) and photo cards inside a place card; every floating chrome surface (search card, map controls, step card, ETA bar) uses blur instead.

RESPONSIVE: iPad collapses the search card into a persistent left sidebar (~360pt) with the map taking the remainder; iPad Pro 13" can show sidebar + map + a right-side place-card pane simultaneously. Phone landscape moves the search card to a left-side panel.
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. Never substitute a custom font for the system typeface family — the entire point of this style is to feel indistinguishable from a first-party OS app, and a custom face immediately breaks that illusion.
2. Use blur-based materials, not solid fills, for anything that floats over the map — a solid card looks like a separate screen bolted onto the map rather than a companion layer above it.
3. Keep the dropped-pin color constant regardless of category — recoloring the pin itself removes the one visual anchor a user can rely on across every kind of search result.
4. Apply tabular figures to every distance, duration, ETA and price — without them, stacked numeric rows visibly jitter and misalign as digits change width.
5. Default to Semibold (600), not Bold (700), for in-context emphasis — reserve true Bold and the rare Heavy weight for the very top of the hierarchy (titles), so lower-level emphasis doesn't compete with headline weight.
6. Never omit the pulse on a live current-location indicator — a static dot reads as "we don't know if this is live," which undermines trust in a location feature.
7. Stack floating action buttons vertically in one corner rather than scattering them — a single predictable cluster is faster to scan under time pressure (e.g. mid-navigation).
8. Keep the search-card's top radius modest (around 10pt) rather than matching the more generous radius used elsewhere in iOS chrome — the search card is meant to read as an extension of the status bar's materials, not a heavy modal.
</house_rules>

<the_project>
Describe your own mapping or location-aware app:
- App name / working title: ____
- What kind of place or route are users searching for (e.g. restaurants, trailheads, transit stops, delivery drop-offs)?: ____
- Do you need turn-by-turn navigation, or just point lookup and directions handoff?: ____
- Any custom category taxonomy beyond food/coffee/shopping/parking?: ____
- Should the primary accent stay iOS system blue, or do you have your own brand color to substitute?: ____
- iPad/multi-pane support needed? (yes/no): ____
- Any live/real-time element beyond user location (e.g. live vehicle position, live queue length)?: ____
</the_project>

<what_to_give_me>
1. **Adapted cartography or surface palette** — if you're skinning a real map, the land/water/park/road tokens above adapted to your brand; if not a literal map, the equivalent "canvas vs. content" surface palette carried over.
2. **Sliding card component** — a full spec or SwiftUI `.sheet` + `.presentationDetents` implementation for your primary search or browse surface, with the three-detent behavior described.
3. **Category/marker system** — your app's pin or marker taxonomy with a universal marker color plus category-specific icon colors, following the "pin stays constant, icon inside varies" rule.
4. **Floating control cluster** — the equivalent of the map-controls stack for your app's persistent utility actions, with exact sizing and blur treatment.
5. **Live-indicator component** — if relevant, a pulsing/animated live-position or live-status indicator with concrete timing values.
6. **Type and tabular-figure guidance** — which of your numeric UI elements (times, distances, counts) must use tabular figures and why.
7. **iPad/large-screen adaptation notes** — how your single-column phone layout should split into sidebar + detail on a bigger canvas.
install: Paste the Starter into Claude alongside a screenshot or description of your current map screen
Fill in the <the_project> fields describing your search unit and marker taxonomy
Ask for the sliding search-card component first — it is the anchor most other screens hang off
Layer in the floating control cluster and any live-position indicator as a second pass
Validate blur-material rendering on a real device, since simulators can misrepresent translucency

name: Booking.com Design System
summary: A reference prompt for Booking.com iOS's dense, conversion-forward marketplace layout, navy/blue role split, and signature review-score badge.
description: Captures the two-blue color discipline, Inter type ramp, and property-card density rules that define Booking.com's iOS app, for building an original travel marketplace.

whatYouGet: The two-blue color discipline (deep navy for brand/structure vs. bright blue for action) plus the single yellow rating accent
Full Inter type ramp with tabular-figure rules for prices and review scores
The signature navy review-score badge format, including its locked one-decimal number rule
Dense property-card anatomy — border-defined rather than shadow-heavy — with exact padding and layout order
Search-form-card, Genius-style loyalty banner, and map price-pin specifications
A border-radius scale that deliberately keeps primary buttons squared rather than pill-shaped
content.promptText:
<role>
You are a product design engineer who has spent years building high-density, conversion-optimized marketplace apps for online travel agencies. You think in terms of information density per screen, trust signals, and a strict, disciplined color role system rather than expressive branding — every pixel on your cards has to earn its place by moving a browsing user toward a completed booking.
</role>

<reference_data>
COLOR ROLES (a two-blue system — do not blur the two):
- Brand/structure navy (app bar, loyalty banner, review-score badge background, logotype): #003580
- Action blue (primary CTA, links, selected filter state, active tab): #0071C2, pressed #005A9C
- Light blue tint (selected filter background, info banners): #E7F0F7
- The single non-blue accent, reserved for star ratings only: #FEBB02
- Canvas: #FFFFFF | Surface/section separator: #F2F2F2 | Divider: #E0E0E0
- Text primary: #1A1A1A | Text secondary (location, metadata): #6B6B6B | Text tertiary (struck-through price, disabled): #949494
- Semantic: success/free-cancellation green #008009, urgency/deal red #CC0000, warning amber #F5A623

TYPE (Inter, weights 400/600/700, tabular figures on all numerals):
- Screen title: 22pt / 700 / -0.3pt
- Property/stay name: 17pt / 700 / -0.1pt
- Price: 17pt / 700, tabular, right-aligned
- Review-score number (inside the badge): 15pt / 700, tabular
- Score word beside the badge ("Fabulous", "Very good"): 14pt / 700
- Body: 15pt / 400 / 1.45 line-height
- Meta/location: 13pt / 400
- Badge/tag: 12pt / 600 / +0.1pt tracking
- Fine print ("Includes taxes and fees"): 11pt / 400 — always shown, never hidden, since visible trust copy is treated as part of the conversion funnel rather than legal clutter

THE SIGNATURE REVIEW-SCORE BADGE: a small solid-navy (#003580) rounded rectangle, 4-6pt corner radius, roughly 30×24pt, containing a white one-decimal score (always formatted X.X — e.g. 8.9, never 8.90 or a bare integer) at 15pt weight 700. Immediately to its right sits a bold word label mapped to the score band (9+ = "Fabulous", 8+ = "Very good", 7+ = "Good") followed by "· N reviews" in secondary gray. This exact format — navy chip, one decimal, word label, count — should never be restyled per screen; treat it as a locked component the way a logo would be locked.

PROPERTY CARD (the core density unit): leading photo (~120pt square or 4:3, 8pt radius) beside a details column; card itself is white, 8pt radius, defined by a 1pt #E0E0E0 border rather than a shadow. Stack order: name (17pt/700) → location link (blue) + distance (gray) → policy line ("Free cancellation" in green) → the review-score badge row → a right-aligned price block (optional struck-through original price, bold discounted total, "Includes taxes and fees" fine print, and an optional red urgency line like "Only 2 rooms left").

SEARCH FORM CARD: a single elevated white card (8pt radius, soft shadow) stacking three 52pt rows — destination, dates, guests — each divided by a hairline, topped by a full-width action-blue "Search" button.

GENIUS-STYLE LOYALTY BANNER: a full-navy strip/card (8pt radius) carrying the loyalty wordmark, a benefit line in white, and an optional yellow discount chip.

MAP TOGGLE + PRICE PINS: a pill floating over the results toggles list/map; unselected pins are white rounded pills with navy text, the selected pin turns solid navy with white text and scales up slightly; tapping a pin slides a single property card up from the bottom.

BORDER RADIUS SCALE (deliberately restrained): tight 4-6pt only for the review badge; standard 8pt for buttons/cards/fields/chips — this INCLUDES primary CTAs, which are squared rather than full pills; comfortable 12pt for sheets; full pill (500pt) reserved for filter chips and the map toggle, not for primary buttons.

ELEVATION: feed cards are border-defined (1pt #E0E0E0), NOT shadow-heavy — shadows are reserved for the few elements that genuinely float above the feed, like the search-form card and the map's floating property card.
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. Keep the two blues role-separated at all times — the deep navy is for brand/structure surfaces, the brighter blue is for anything tappable; mixing them removes the visual cue that tells a user "this is decoration" versus "this is a button."
2. Never restyle the review-score badge per screen or per feature — its rigid navy-chip-plus-one-decimal format is the single most recognizable element in this system, and any variation reads as a bug rather than a design choice.
3. Always format a review score to exactly one decimal place — never a bare integer, never two decimals — because the format itself has become a recognizable signal independent of the number inside it.
4. Define dense list cards with a 1pt border rather than a drop shadow — in a marketplace where dozens of cards may be visible at once, shadows accumulate into visual noise that a border does not.
5. Never hide trust copy (cancellation policy, taxes/fees disclosure) behind a tap — surfacing it inline, even at a small 11pt size, is treated as part of what converts a browser into a booker, not as legal boilerplate to bury.
6. Keep primary call-to-action buttons on the standard 8pt squared radius, not a full pill — reserve pill shapes for filter chips and toggles so that the one shape people should associate with "submit" stays visually distinct from the many shapes used for "refine."
7. Use tabular figures for every price, score, and "only N left" count — a dense list of numbers that individually jitter in width as they update looks unfinished.
8. Reserve the one non-blue accent color strictly for star ratings — introducing it anywhere else dilutes its meaning and adds a third competing hue to an otherwise disciplined two-blue system.
</house_rules>

<the_project>
Describe your own marketplace app so this dense, conversion-forward system can be adapted:
- App name / working title: ____
- What is being listed and booked (e.g. properties, tickets, rental cars, restaurant tables)?: ____
- Do you have an existing review or rating mechanism, and what scale does it use (5-star, 10-point, thumbs)?: ____
- Your brand's structural color (navy-equivalent) and action color (bright-blue-equivalent), if already defined: ____
- Do you run a loyalty or membership program that needs its own banner treatment?: ____
- Do results need a map-toggle view with price pins?: ____
- What urgency or scarcity signals (if any) are legitimate for your product (e.g. "3 left," "12 people viewing")?: ____
</the_project>

<what_to_give_me>
1. **Two-role color token set** — your brand's structural and action colors mapped onto the navy/blue split above, plus the single non-blue accent if you have a rating mechanism.
2. **Adapted review/rating badge component** — a locked, reusable badge spec for your own rating scale, following the "format never varies" rule.
3. **Dense list-card component** — full anatomy for your core listing unit, written as a SwiftUI view or component spec, using border-not-shadow definition.
4. **Search/entry-point card** — the stacked-rows search form pattern adapted to your booking flow's actual fields.
5. **Loyalty or membership banner** (if applicable) — a full-width brand-color strip with the benefit copy and any discount chip.
6. **Map/list toggle spec** (if applicable) — pin states (default/selected/viewed) and the bottom-card reveal interaction.
7. **A short list of urgency/trust-copy rules** — which scarcity cues are honest for your product and where trust copy must remain visible rather than hidden.
install: Paste the Starter into Claude with a note on what your app lists and books
Fill in the <the_project> fields, especially your rating scale and structural/action colors
Request the review-score badge component first since most other components reference it
Build the dense list-card next, then the search-form card and any loyalty banner
Cross-check your final CTA radius against the house rule — it should stay squared, not pill-shaped

name: Citymapper Design System
summary: A reference prompt for Citymapper iOS's theme-invariant transit-mode color system, colored leg-strip routes, and the locked green GO button.
description: Captures the mode-color palette, leg-strip route visualization, and the shape/color-locked GO action button that define Citymapper's iOS transit app.

whatYouGet: The full theme-invariant transit-mode color palette (walk, bus, tube, rail, bike, cab, ferry) that never changes between light and dark
The locked GO button specification — shape, color and label held identical across every screen and theme
Leg-strip route-visualization anatomy: colored mode chips with directional arrows between them
Origin-to-destination card, departures board, and disruption-banner component specs
A chunky, extra-bold type ramp built for glanceable reading while in motion
Motion and haptic timing for route selection, GO-mode start, and live departure countdowns
content.promptText:
<role>
You are an iOS design engineer specializing in real-time public transit and multimodal journey-planning apps. You believe a route should be readable in under a second from color alone, and you treat certain controls in your app as brand-locked constants that must never be re-themed or re-shaped no matter what screen they appear on.
</role>

<reference_data>
THEME-INVARIANT TRANSIT-MODE COLORS (these do NOT change between light and dark mode — a bus is always red regardless of theme):
- Walk: #00B894 | Bus: #E8453C | Tube/Metro/Subway: #2B5BFF | Rail/Train: #8E44D8 | Bike/Scooter: #00A8C5 | Cab/Rideshare: #FFB400 | Ferry: #0094C6
- Rule: when the real transit agency's own official line color is known (e.g. a specific subway line), it overrides the generic mode-category color; the mode color is the fallback and category default only.

BRAND/INTERACTIVE COLORS:
- Brand accent (destination pin, primary links, selected states, also doubles as the metro mode color): #2B5BFF, bright dark-mode variant #4D7BFF, pressed #1E45CC
- The GO action color, reserved exclusively for the GO button and its full-screen live-navigation mode — never used for any other UI: #00C281
- Disruption/delay-alert orange: #FF8A00 | Cancelled/severe-delay red: #E8453C (shares the bus red intentionally, since red already means "stop/problem")

CANVAS: light canvas #FFFFFF / surface #F4F5F8 / divider #E3E5EC; dark canvas #0C0E14 (a deep blue-black, deliberately NOT pure black) / surface #15171F / divider #282C38

TYPE (a chunky, confident geometric grotesque; Inter at weights 400-900 is the closest free substitute; tabular figures mandatory on anything that counts down):
- Display: 32pt / weight 900 / -0.5pt tracking
- ETA hero (the number a user acts on): 26pt / 800
- Row title: 18pt / 700
- Mode badge (uppercase, on a colored chip): 12pt / 800 / +0.3pt tracking
- GO button label: 18pt / 900 / +0.4pt tracking, uppercase
- Route tag pill ("Fastest", "Cheapest"): 10pt / 800 uppercase
- Principle: the number you are meant to act on (an ETA, a countdown, the GO label) is always the loudest, heaviest type on the screen — everything descriptive stays regular-weight gray.

THE LEG STRIP (the signature route visualization — never render a route as plain text): a horizontal row of colored mode chips, each an 8-10pt-radius pill in its mode color containing a small white glyph plus a short label (a duration for a walk leg, a line name for a transit leg), separated by a muted directional arrow. A route is read by its sequence of colors before its words are read at all.

THE GO BUTTON (shape- and color-locked everywhere — treat exactly like a logo, never contextual): a full rounded pill, corner radius ≈ half its own height, roughly 54pt tall, solid #00C281 fill, containing a play-triangle glyph and the word "GO" in the heaviest weight available, with a green-tinted glow shadow beneath it. It must render identically on every screen and in both light and dark themes — no exceptions, no seasonal reskins.

ORIGIN→DESTINATION CARD: a rounded container holding two stacked rows — a muted gray dot for "from," a brand-blue dot for "to" — connected by a short vertical line segment, deliberately evoking a transit-map stop pair.

DEPARTURES BOARD: a live, auto-refreshing list; each row has a small colored line badge, a destination name, and a countdown in minutes that is normally shown in the GO-green color but flips to the disruption-orange color once it drops to 3 minutes or fewer ("leave now" urgency).

DISRUPTION BANNER: an inline orange strip inside route results (never hidden in a sub-screen) carrying a warning glyph and a short delay/closure description; severe closures escalate to the cancelled-red color instead of orange.

MOTION: a route-list bottom sheet drags 1:1 with the finger between peek/half/full snap points; starting GO mode cross-dissolves the screen over ~350ms while a progress line draws in over ~500ms; departure countdowns decrement with a ~150ms number cross-fade, animating to the orange threshold color over ~200ms when they cross into the "imminent" band.
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. Never let a transit mode change color based on light/dark theme — a bus must read as the same red in every lighting condition, because the whole point of the mode-color system is instant, unambiguous recognition.
2. Render every route as a colored leg strip, never as a plain text description — a route with no visual color sequence forces the user to actually read it, which defeats the glanceable design goal.
3. Treat the primary live-action button (the GO-equivalent) as shape- and color-locked across the entire app — if a designer wants to "refresh" its look for a promotion or a seasonal theme, that request should be declined, because consistency here is what makes it instantly findable under stress.
4. Reserve your single "go/live/success" green for that one meaning only — introducing a second green anywhere else in the UI creates ambiguity about whether something is actionable right now.
5. Never let disruption or delay information live only on a secondary screen — surface it inline, in its warning color, directly in the results a user is already looking at.
6. Use tabular figures for every live-updating number (countdowns, ETAs, minutes) so that as digits change width, nothing in a stacked list visibly shifts or jitters.
7. Keep descriptive/supporting text at a normal weight even while the loudest numeric data on the same screen sits at the very top of the weight scale — the contrast between the two is what makes the important number pop without needing extra color or size.
8. Default to color-plus-icon-plus-label for every mode indicator, never color alone — color-blind users and VoiceOver both need the glyph and text to carry the same information the color does.
</house_rules>

<the_project>
Describe your own real-time transit, delivery, or journey-planning app:
- App name / working title: ____
- What are the "modes" or transport legs a route might combine (e.g. walk, e-bike, rideshare, shuttle, courier)?: ____
- What is your equivalent of the GO button — the one live-action control that should be locked in shape and color everywhere?: ____
- Your brand accent color, if distinct from your primary mode color: ____
- Do you have live countdowns or ETAs that need an "imminent" threshold color change?: ____
- Do you need a disruption/delay-alert mechanism, and what should trigger it?: ____
- Bottom tab structure: ____
</the_project>

<what_to_give_me>
1. **Mode-color palette** — a theme-invariant color assignment for every transport mode or leg type in your product, with a rule for when a real-world identifier (like an official line color) should override the default.
2. **Leg-strip component** — a SwiftUI view or component spec rendering your own multi-leg routes as colored chips with arrows between them.
3. **The locked primary-action button** — full spec (shape, color, label, shadow, and haptic) for your app's GO-equivalent, explicitly marked as never re-themeable.
4. **Origin/destination or start/end input card** — adapted to your product's actual start and end concepts.
5. **Live countdown or status list** — your equivalent of the departures board, including the threshold rule for switching to an urgency color.
6. **Disruption/alert banner** — inline, in-context alert component for delays or problems, with a severity escalation path.
7. **Motion and haptic table** — concrete durations and easing for your version of route selection, the primary-action start, and any live countdown.
install: Paste the Starter into Claude along with a description of your app's transport modes or route legs
Fill in the <the_project> fields, especially your GO-equivalent action and mode taxonomy
Ask for the mode-color palette and leg-strip component first, since nearly everything else depends on them
Add the locked primary-action button as its own explicitly non-negotiable component
Layer in the departures/countdown list and disruption banner once the core route view is settled

name: Delta Design System
summary: A reference prompt for Fly Delta iOS's navy-grounded, status-first concierge layout centered on the digital boarding pass and flight-status timeline.
description: Captures the disciplined navy/red color roles, Whitney-class type ramp, and boarding-pass anatomy that define Delta's iOS app, for an original airline or travel-status build.

whatYouGet: The disciplined navy/red color role split — brand-anchor navy versus a single, sparingly-used high-energy CTA red
A functional flight-status palette (on-time, boarding, delayed, cancelled) kept deliberately separate from brand color
Full anatomy of the signature digital boarding pass: gradient strip, passenger row, Gate/Seat/Group grid, and barcode block
The vertical flight-status timeline pattern (Departed → In Air → Arrive) with dot-and-rail styling
A bold, humanist type ramp built for scanning gate/seat/time data under travel-day stress
Dark-mode notes including the barcode-inversion rule so a gate scanner can still read a dimmed screen
content.promptText:
<role>
You are an iOS design engineer who has built travel-status and boarding-document experiences for a major airline, and who thinks about every screen in terms of "does this reduce travel anxiety." You default to a calm navy brand color, reserve your one high-energy accent for a single call-to-action per screen, and treat your boarding-document surface as the single most important artifact in the entire app.
</role>

<reference_data>
COLOR ROLES (deliberately disciplined — do not let these blur into each other):
- Brand/navigation anchor (a deep, trustworthy navy): #003268, with a brighter secondary-CTA variant #0F4C9A for use on dark surfaces
- The single high-energy accent, reserved almost exclusively for the primary call-to-action on a screen (never a decorative accent): #C8102E, pressed #A30D26
- Loyalty/status accent, used ONLY for tier badges and loyalty-program emphasis: #C99700 (gold)
- Canvas: #FFFFFF light / a deep NAVY-CHARCOAL #0B1320 in dark mode — never neutral black, because the brand navy needs to keep reading even in the dark theme
- Surface gray: #F4F6F9 | Divider: #D6DCE7
- Text primary: #10243F (a navy-tinted near-black, not pure black) | secondary: #5A6A82

FUNCTIONAL FLIGHT-STATUS COLORS (kept deliberately distinct from brand color so status is never confused with decoration): on-time green #1E8E5A, boarding blue #0F4C9A, delayed amber #C99700, cancelled/error red #C8102E, gate-changed orange #D9730D. Each has a brighter dark-mode variant (e.g. on-time becomes #4FD18C on dark).

TYPE (a humanist sans in the Whitney/Open-Sans family; weight ladder concentrates on 400/600/700/800; tabular figures mandatory on gate/seat/time data):
- Route/airport code (the trip hero): 34pt / weight 800 / -0.5pt tracking
- Screen title: 26pt / 800
- Data-grid value (Gate/Seat/Group cell): 22pt / 800
- Passenger name on the pass (uppercase): 18pt / 700
- Body: 16pt / 400 / 1.5 line-height
- Eyebrow/label ("TODAY · flight number", uppercase): 12pt / 700 / +0.6pt tracking
- Cell label ("GATE"/"SEAT"/"GROUP", uppercase): 10pt / 700 / +0.6pt tracking
- Principle: the data a traveler scans under stress (airport codes, gate, seat, group, times) is always the largest and heaviest type on the screen — labels are uppercase with wide tracking, content stays normally cased.

THE DIGITAL BOARDING PASS (the signature surface — the highest-elevation, most-detailed card in the app): a tall container, 18pt corner radius, topped by a thin 6pt gradient strip running from the brand navy into the CTA red. Below: a "PASSENGER" label over the traveler's name in uppercase; then a three-cell equal-width grid — Gate / Seat / Group — each cell a small uppercase label over a large bold value (the Group/loyalty-tier value may render in the gold accent); then a full-width rounded "zone band" strip stating the boarding time and boarding zone; then a tall barcode block at the very bottom. On dark mode the barcode block INVERTS to a light bar pattern on a dark ground, specifically so a gate scanner can still read a dimmed phone screen.

FLIGHT-STATUS TIMELINE (the second signature surface, sitting above the pass): a card containing a vertical rail of small dots connected by thin bars — completed/active steps get a filled status-color dot with a ring, upcoming steps get a muted gray dot — each paired with a bold step title ("Departed [city] — On Time") and a lighter metadata line (gate and time). The in-progress step's dot pulses gently.

STATUS CHIPS: rounded-pill chips, bold uppercase-feeling label, tinted background matching the functional status color at low opacity (e.g. green text on a pale green fill for "On Time").

TRIP HERO (the "what's happening right now" header): a full-bleed navy gradient block showing a small uppercase eyebrow ("TODAY · flight number"), a status pill in the top-right, and a large route row — big bold origin code, an animated plane glyph gliding along a thin connecting line, big bold destination code.

BORDER RADIUS: mostly a restrained 6pt on buttons/fields, 16pt on list/timeline cards, and a distinct larger 18pt reserved for the boarding pass itself — signaling that the pass is a different, more important category of surface than an ordinary card.

ELEVATION: mostly flat, with purposeful elevation concentrated on the boarding pass (the single most-elevated surface in the app) and on floating actions; on the dark navy-charcoal canvas, shadows nearly vanish, so a thin divider-colored border doubles as the elevation cue instead.
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. Reserve your single high-energy accent color for exactly one primary call-to-action per screen — using it decoratively anywhere else dilutes its meaning as "the one thing to tap right now."
2. Keep functional status colors (on-time/delayed/cancelled) completely separate from brand color, even when both happen to be similar hues — conflating "this is Delta blue" with "this flight is currently boarding" creates a genuinely confusing reading for a stressed traveler.
3. Give your boarding-document or ticket surface the highest visual elevation and most generous internal padding in the entire app — it is the artifact a user physically holds up to a scanner, so it should look and feel like the most important object on screen.
4. Size and weight the data a user scans under time pressure (gate, seat, times, codes) as the loudest content on any screen — never render this data in small or light type just because it's "just metadata."
5. Never use a neutral or pure-black canvas for dark mode when your brand color is a saturated hue like navy — a slightly tinted dark canvas keeps the brand identity alive even in the dark theme.
6. Invert any scannable machine-readable element (barcode, QR code) to a light-on-dark pattern specifically in dark mode, because a screen dimmed for battery or nighttime use must remain readable by a scanner.
7. Uppercase only labels and eyebrows, never passenger-entered or otherwise cased content — this keeps the visual grammar of "this is a system label" distinct from "this is your data."
8. Keep motion calm and purely functional (a status color cross-fade, a gentle pulse, a plane gliding along a line) — avoid decorative bounce or playful easing, since this is a trust-and-logistics tool, not an entertainment app.
</house_rules>

<the_project>
Describe your own status-first travel or logistics app:
- App name / working title: ____
- What is the core "document" or credential your user holds up or references (e.g. a boarding pass, a ticket, a delivery confirmation)?: ____
- What are the stages of your status timeline (e.g. Departed → In Air → Arrive, or Ordered → Packed → Shipped → Delivered)?: ____
- Your brand's navy-equivalent structural color and your single CTA accent color, if already defined: ____
- Do you have a loyalty or tier program that needs its own accent color?: ____
- Does your document need to be scanned by a machine (barcode/QR), and does it need a dark-mode inversion rule?: ____
- Bottom tab structure: ____
</the_project>

<what_to_give_me>
1. **Disciplined color role set** — your brand structural color, single CTA accent, and functional status palette, explicitly kept separate the way the reference system does.
2. **Signature document/card component** — full anatomy for your core credential or status artifact, written as a SwiftUI view or component spec, including any scannable element and its dark-mode behavior.
3. **Status timeline component** — a vertical dot-and-rail timeline adapted to your own stages, with completed/active/upcoming states defined.
4. **Status chip set** — pill-shaped chips for each of your functional states, each with a text and tint-background color pairing.
5. **Hero/header component** — a "what matters right now" header block for your app's home or primary tab.
6. **Type ramp** — your app's hierarchy from hero data through body through uppercase labels, with weight and tracking specified per role.
7. **A short calm-motion note** — 3-5 named motion moments (status change, document reveal, live update) with concrete, restrained timing.
install: Paste the Starter into Claude with a note describing your core document/credential and status stages
Fill in the <the_project> fields, especially your navy-equivalent and single accent colors
Request the signature document component first — it anchors most of the visual language
Add the status timeline and status-chip set as the next layer
If your document needs to be scanned, explicitly confirm the dark-mode inversion behavior before shipping

name: Expedia Design System
summary: A reference prompt for Expedia iOS's deal-forward marketplace layout, role-bound yellow/blue/navy/gold color system, and property-result-card anatomy.
description: Captures the four-color role discipline, Expedia Sans type ramp, and savings-forward card pattern that define Expedia's iOS app, for building an original deal-driven travel marketplace.

whatYouGet: A strict four-color role system: savings/deal yellow, interactive blue, brand/trust navy, and a rewards-only gold, each scoped to one job
The full property-result-card anatomy: hero photo, deal flag, save-heart, review-score badge, strikethrough-to-discounted price block, and a rewards-earn line
A score-band color ramp for the review-score badge that shifts hue with score tier
Segmented search-mode switch and single search-pill entry-point specifications
The bundle/save promotional module pattern and a rewards-balance strip component
Motion notes including a brief accent-color flash to signal a price drop
content.promptText:
<role>
You are a growth-focused iOS product designer who has built deal-driven travel or e-commerce marketplaces where the entire point of a results screen is to surface a compelling price. You work in a strict color-role discipline — every accent color in your palette has exactly one job, and you never let two of them share a meaning.
</role>

<reference_data>
FOUR-COLOR ROLE SYSTEM (each color has exactly one job — do not let them overlap):
- Savings/deal/loyalty-highlight yellow, used ONLY for deal flags, member-price tags, and the highest-intent "bundle and save" call-to-action (text on it is always the brand navy, never white): #FFC94D, pressed/deep variant #FFB31A
- Interactive action blue, used for the primary reserve/booking button, links, and selected states (white text on it): #1668E3, pressed #0F4FB0
- Brand/trust navy, used for the logo field, review-badge backgrounds, and dark header overlays: #00355F
- Rewards-only gold, used exclusively for a loyalty-points balance and "earn X points" lines — never for generic UI: #F5C518

CANVAS: near-white #FFFFFF / surface #F5F7FA light; a navy-biased dark charcoal #0E1116 in dark mode (never pure black, so the brand's navy identity still reads); divider #E3E7ED light / #2A323E dark

TYPE (a geometric humanist sans; Inter is the closest free substitute; weight concentrates at 400/600/700/800; tabular figures mandatory on all prices and scores):
- Display (home hero): 32pt / weight 800 / -0.6pt tracking
- Card/property title: 18pt / 700
- Discounted "now" price (the loudest non-display element on the whole screen): 18pt / 800
- Review-score number inside its badge: 15pt / 800
- Strikethrough antecedent price: 13pt / 400
- Deal flag / badge text: 12pt / 600
- Rewards-earn line: 11pt / 700
- Principle: text on the savings-yellow accent is always the brand navy, and text on the interactive blue is always white — this pairing rule is treated as fixed, not a per-screen choice.

SCORE-BAND COLOR RAMP for the review-score badge (background shifts with score, always paired with a word label to its right):
- 9.0-10 (top tier): a success green background
- 8.0-8.9: the interactive blue background
- 7.0-7.9: a muted navy background
- 6.0-6.9: neutral gray
- below 6.0: a lighter neutral gray

THE PROPERTY/RESULT CARD (the workhorse component, repeated for stays, fares, and cars): a white (dark-mode-surface) card, 16pt radius, thin divider border, subtle shadow. A full-width photo at roughly a 16:10 ratio tops the card, carrying a small yellow "deal flag" chip in the top-left corner (bundle discount or member-price callout, navy text) and a save-heart icon in the top-right corner over a semi-transparent dark circle for contrast. Below the photo: the title, then a secondary location line, then the review-score badge row (score + word + review count), then the price block — an optional strikethrough original price, the bold discounted price, and a "/ night" or similar suffix — and finally a rewards-earn line marked with a small gold dot or coin glyph, kept in its own visual lane rather than crowded against other copy.

SEGMENTED SEARCH-MODE SWITCH: a row of equal-width pill segments (e.g. Stays / Flights / Cars / Bundle); the inactive segments use a neutral surface fill and secondary text, while the active segment fills with the savings-yellow accent and navy text — the highest-intent mode gets the yellow treatment, not blue.

SEARCH PILL: a rounded, shadowed entry point showing a two-line summary (destination on one line, dates/traveler count on the second, smaller and secondary-colored) with a leading search-glyph.

BUNDLE/SAVE MODULE: a stacked promotional block showing individual component prices (each struck through) collapsing into one combined, discounted "bundle" price, headed by a savings figure rendered in navy text over a pale-yellow band, and closed with a yellow "bundle and save" button — deliberately yellow rather than blue, since this is the single highest-intent conversion action in the app.

REWARDS-BALANCE STRIP: a rounded surface row with a leading gold coin glyph, a title/subtitle pair, and a trailing bold gold balance figure — appears wherever a loyalty balance is relevant (home, checkout, account).

MOTION: when a price drops (e.g. after a date change), the old price cross-dissolves into the new one and the price briefly flashes the savings-yellow color before settling back to the normal text color — a small, deliberate signal that something got cheaper.
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. Never use your savings/deal accent color for generic chrome, body text, or anything that isn't actually a saving — every use of that color should mean "this is cheaper than it could be," and diluting it into decoration breaks that promise.
2. Enforce the text-pairing rule strictly: navy text on the savings-yellow background, white text on the interactive-blue background — treat this as a fixed pairing, not a per-screen styling choice, since an inverted pairing both fails contrast and confuses the color's meaning.
3. Reserve your rewards/loyalty accent color exclusively for balances and "earn" lines — it should never appear as a generic icon tint or body accent, because its entire value is signaling "this is your loyalty currency" at a glance.
4. Never show a strikethrough "was" price unless there is a genuinely real discount behind it — a fake-looking strikethrough undermines trust in every other price on the screen.
5. Always front-load the review-score badge (score, word label, review count) near the top of a result card — it is a primary trust signal and should never be buried below less important details.
6. Give the highest-intent conversion action (e.g. a bundle/save button) your savings-accent color rather than your standard interactive-blue color — this reinforces that the action itself is a savings opportunity, not just "another button."
7. Use a navy-biased dark canvas rather than a neutral or pure black one — keeping a hint of the brand's navy alive in dark mode preserves brand recognition even when the whole app inverts.
8. Keep motion functional and brief (180-320ms) — a short color flash to indicate a price change is appropriate, but avoid decorative or bouncy animation that would distract from the commercial information on screen.
</house_rules>

<the_project>
Describe your own deal-driven marketplace app:
- App name / working title: ____
- What is being sold (e.g. stays, flights, event tickets, retail bundles)?: ____
- Do you have a rating/review mechanism, and on what scale?: ____
- Do you have a loyalty/points program that needs its own reserved accent color?: ____
- Your brand's savings-accent color and interactive-action color, if already defined: ____
- Do you offer bundling or package deals across multiple product types?: ____
- Search-mode segments (e.g. product categories) users switch between: ____
</the_project>

<what_to_give_me>
1. **Four-role color token set** — your savings accent, interactive accent, brand/trust color, and rewards-only accent, each scoped to a single job the way the reference system enforces.
2. **Result/property card component** — full anatomy adapted to your product, written as a SwiftUI view or component spec, including deal flag, save affordance, rating badge, and price block.
3. **Score-band badge system** — your own rating scale mapped onto a color ramp with word labels per tier.
4. **Segmented mode switch** — adapted to your own product categories, with the active-state color rule specified.
5. **Bundle/promotional module** (if applicable) — a savings-forward component showing individual vs. combined pricing.
6. **Rewards-balance strip** (if applicable) — a loyalty-balance component using only the reserved rewards color.
7. **Price-change motion spec** — the exact color-flash and cross-fade behavior for your app's price-update moments.
install: Paste the Starter into Claude describing what your marketplace sells and whether it bundles products
Fill in the <the_project> fields, especially your four color roles if you already have brand colors
Request the property/result-card component first, since it is reused across product types
Add the score-band badge and segmented mode switch as the next components
If you run a loyalty program, explicitly confirm the rewards accent is never used outside that context

name: Flighty Design System
summary: A reference prompt for Flighty iOS's deep-black instrument-panel aesthetic, single blue accent, and glowing live great-circle flight-map arc.
description: Captures the near-black canvas, strict status-color semantics, and live-arc map visualization that define Flighty's iOS flight-tracking app, for an original real-time tracking build.

whatYouGet: The deep-black instrument-panel canvas and layered dark-surface ramp, with a rule against ever using true pure black
A single-accent color discipline plus strictly-scoped status colors (on-time green, delay amber, cancelled red) used only on chips and timelines
Full anatomy of the live-arc flight map: glowing great-circle path, plane marker, and draw-in animation timing
The flight-card component: route codes, hero-sized times, gate/terminal readout, and a status chip
A Live-Activity-style persistent status bar and an on-time-percentage ring component
Tabular-figure and Dynamic Type rules tuned for data that updates live without visually jittering
content.promptText:
<role>
You are an iOS design engineer who specializes in real-time data-tracking apps built around a single, near-black "instrument panel" canvas. You believe restraint in your color palette is what makes a single glowing accent color read as unmistakably significant, and you design every numeric readout to survive live updates without ever visually jittering.
</role>

<reference_data>
CANVAS AND SURFACE RAMP (deep, near-black — never true pure black, since a totally black canvas swallows depth cues entirely):
- Canvas: #0B0B0F | Surface 1 (cards): #1A1A1F | Surface 2 (sheets, elevated rows): #222228 | Surface 3 (pressed state): #2C2C34 | Divider: #2E2E36
- Text primary: #FFFFFF | Text secondary: #8E8E96 | Text tertiary/disabled: #5A5A62

SINGLE ACCENT (the only non-status color in the entire palette): #0A84FF, pressed #0066CC, with a soft glow halo at roughly 45% opacity used behind the live map arc and its plane marker

STRICT STATUS SEMANTICS (used ONLY on status chips, timeline nodes, and a live progress bar — never decoratively): on-time green #30D158, delay amber #FFD60A, cancelled/diverted red #FF453A. Beyond the single accent and these three status colors, the entire palette is grayscale by design — this restraint is what makes the status colors instantly legible.

TYPE (a precise technical sans; the system font is used directly in production; weight concentrates at 400/600/700 with no thin or black weights; tabular figures are mandatory on every piece of flight data):
- Hero time (departure/arrival, the single largest element on a flight card): 32pt / weight 700 / tabular
- Route/airport code: 24pt / 700 / +0.5pt tracking (a slight positive tracking gives codes a technical, spaced-out read)
- Card title (airline + flight number): 17pt / 600
- Status chip text: 13pt / 700 / +0.3pt tracking, uppercase
- Gate/terminal readout: 15pt / 600, monospaced-feel tabular figures
- On-time percentage (inside its ring): 20pt / 700 / tabular
- Principle: color, not weight, is what signals status — the chip's background/text color carries the meaning, so don't try to also convey urgency through bolder type.

THE LIVE FLIGHT-MAP ARC (the single most important visual in the entire app — the map exists purely to host this): a great-circle path drawn over a dark map, its flown portion rendered as a solid glowing accent-color line and its remaining portion as a dimmed dashed line in the same hue. A plane glyph sits at the live position, rotated to match heading, with its own soft glow halo. On appearing, the arc draws in from the origin to the current live position over roughly 900ms with an ease-out curve, and the glow fades in alongside it. The plane's position should always interpolate smoothly along the curve — it must glide continuously, never jump in discrete steps.

THE FLIGHT CARD: a dark surface-1 card, 16pt radius, thin divider border, deep soft shadow (needed because shadows must work harder to register against a near-black canvas). Header row: airline + flight number, with a trailing status chip. Center: origin code — a thin accent-colored arc-with-plane glyph — destination code, all in the route-code style. Below that: departure and arrival hero times side by side (each the largest text on the card), with a smaller tabular gate/terminal line beneath each. A final meta line gives duration, distance, and stop count in secondary gray.

STATUS CHIP: a full pill shape, uppercase bold text in one of the three strict status colors, sitting on a low-opacity tint of that same color — this is always the fastest-read element on any flight card.

LIVE-ACTIVITY-STYLE STATUS BAR: a persistent, higher-elevation strip mirroring a lock-screen live-activity layout — airline/flight identity on the left, a horizontal origin-to-destination progress track with a moving plane indicator in the center, and a status chip plus ETA on the right.

ON-TIME PERCENTAGE RING: a small circular progress indicator (thin stroke, on-time-green fill against a divider-colored track) with a centered percentage figure and a small "on time" caption beneath it.

DELAY TIMELINE: a vertical rail of small colored dots (one per status color) connected by thin divider-colored bars, each paired with a monospaced timestamp, a bold event title, and a colored delta (e.g. "+22m"); the most recent node pulses gently in its status color.

ELEVATION: because the canvas is so dark, shadows must be deep and soft (roughly 40% opacity, wide blur) simply to register at all — the arc's glow is the one deliberately colored light source in the entire interface, everything else relies on layered dark surfaces rather than heavy shadow.
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. Never substitute a true pure-black canvas for the slightly-lifted near-black one — a totally black background removes the subtle depth cues that make layered dark surfaces readable, and it also makes a glowing accent color look harsh rather than warm.
2. Keep status colors (on-time/delay/cancelled) strictly scoped to chips, timeline nodes, and progress indicators — never use them decoratively elsewhere, because their entire value is that seeing that color anywhere in the app means exactly one specific thing.
3. Reserve the single accent color for the primary action, the live map arc, and active/selected states only — introducing a second accent hue would compete with the map arc for the user's attention, which should always be the visual focal point.
4. Use tabular (fixed-width) figures for every piece of live flight data — times, gate, terminal, on-time percentage — because proportional figures visibly shift and jitter as digits change during a live update.
5. Animate a live position marker as a continuous glide along its path, never as discrete jumps between waypoints — a stepped motion reads as buggy or stale, while a smooth glide reads as "this is genuinely live."
6. Give your hero numeric data (the departure/arrival time, or your app's equivalent primary readout) the single largest and boldest type treatment on any given screen — it is the reason the user opened the app.
7. Use deep, soft shadows rather than crisp ones on a near-black canvas — a subtle, low-opacity shadow simply disappears against very dark surfaces, so depth needs a wider blur radius and higher opacity than it would on a light canvas.
8. Never rely on color alone to convey status for accessibility — pair every status color with a text label (and a VoiceOver-readable string) stating the status in words.
</house_rules>

<the_project>
Describe your own live-tracking or real-time-status app:
- App name / working title: ____
- What is being tracked in real time (e.g. a flight, a delivery, a live event, a vehicle)?: ____
